scenes.headline: 10 currencies that collapsed
scenes.body: Hungary. Zimbabwe. Germany. Venezuela. And six more.
scenes.voiceover: In nineteen forty-six, prices in Hungary doubled every fifteen hours. A salary paid on Monday morning had lost about ninety percent of its value by Wednesday.

scenes.headline: Speed, scale and lasting damage
scenes.voiceover: These are the ten worst currency failures in history, ranked by how fast prices rose, how far the money fell, and how long the damage lasted. For each one: how bad it got, and what caused it.

scenes.headline: Polish marka
scenes.voiceover: Number ten. The Polish marka. Poland.

scenes.name: Polish marka
scenes.headline: Millions of marks to one dollar
scenes.voiceover: After the First World War, a US dollar cost about nine Polish marks. By late nineteen twenty-three it cost millions. At the peak, prices rose two hundred and seventy-five percent in a single month.

scenes.name: Polish marka
scenes.headline: A new country with no money to run it
scenes.body: Poland was rebuilt from three war-ruined pieces, then fought the 1920 Polish–Soviet war on printed money.
scenes.voiceover: Poland had just been rebuilt from three territories ruined by war. It paid for its government, and for the Polish–Soviet war of nineteen twenty, by printing money. In nineteen twenty-four the marka was replaced by the złoty, at one point eight million marks each.

scenes.headline: Nationalist Chinese yuan
scenes.voiceover: Number nine. The Nationalist Chinese yuan. China.

scenes.name: Nationalist Chinese yuan
scenes.headline: A brand-new currency, dead within months

stat.label: Time for prices to double, April 1949

scenes.voiceover: By April nineteen forty-nine, prices in China were doubling roughly every five days. A new gold yuan, launched in nineteen forty-eight to fix the problem, collapsed within months.

scenes.name: Nationalist Chinese yuan
scenes.headline: Paying for a civil war with the printing press
scenes.body: The government printed money to fight Mao's communists as its tax base shrank.
scenes.voiceover: The Nationalist government was fighting a civil war against Mao Zedong's communists, and paid for most of it by printing money, while the territory it could tax kept shrinking. Many historians see the hyperinflation as one reason the Nationalists lost mainland China.

scenes.headline: Confidence lost
scenes.body: When people stop trusting money, they spend it as fast as they can.
scenes.voiceover: Once people expect money to lose value, they spend it the moment they get it. That makes prices rise even faster.

scenes.headline: Argentine peso
scenes.voiceover: Number eight. The Argentine peso. Argentina.

scenes.name: Argentine peso
scenes.headline: Two collapses in one generation
scenes.voiceover: In July nineteen eighty-nine, prices in Argentina rose nearly two hundred percent in one month. Then, in two thousand and two, the peso, which had been fixed at one to the US dollar, crashed to nearly four.

scenes.name: Argentine peso
scenes.headline: Deficits, then a peg that couldn't hold
scenes.body: Chronic deficits funded by the central bank, then a rigid dollar peg that broke in 2002.
scenes.voiceover: For decades, the central bank funded government deficits. A fixed one-to-one dollar peg in nineteen ninety-one stopped inflation, but made the economy uncompetitive. In two thousand and one came a bank run, a freeze on withdrawals, and what was then the biggest government debt default in history.

scenes.headline: Confederate dollar
scenes.voiceover: Number seven. The Confederate dollar. Confederate States.

scenes.name: Confederate dollar
scenes.headline: Money backed by a war it lost
scenes.voiceover: By the end of the American Civil War, prices in the Confederate South were about ninety times higher than in eighteen sixty-one.

scenes.name: Confederate dollar
scenes.headline: A war paid for with paper
scenes.body: The South had little industry to tax, and the Union blockade choked its cotton exports.
scenes.voiceover: The South had little industry to tax, and the Union naval blockade choked off its cotton exports. So it paid for the war mostly by printing money. When the Confederacy lost, its dollars became worthless.

scenes.headline: Cotton couldn't save it
scenes.body: The blockade cut off the South's biggest export.
scenes.voiceover: Cotton was the South's great export, and the blockade cut it off.

scenes.headline: Soviet and Russian rouble
scenes.voiceover: Number six. The Soviet and Russian rouble. USSR to Russia.

scenes.name: Soviet and Russian rouble
scenes.headline: Life savings wiped out in a year
scenes.voiceover: When Russia freed prices in January nineteen ninety-two, prices jumped two hundred and forty-five percent in that month alone. Over the year, consumer prices rose about two thousand five hundred percent, and Soviet-era savings were wiped out.

scenes.name: Soviet and Russian rouble
scenes.headline: An empire ends, the printing press doesn't
scenes.body: Late-Soviet deficits were funded by printing. Then price controls ended overnight.
scenes.voiceover: In the last years of the Soviet Union, the government covered growing deficits by printing roubles, while price controls hid the damage. When the Soviet Union broke up and prices were freed, years of pent-up inflation hit at once.

scenes.headline: Venezuelan bolívar
scenes.voiceover: Number five. The Venezuelan bolívar. Venezuela.

scenes.name: Venezuelan bolívar
scenes.headline: Fourteen zeros removed
scenes.voiceover: Venezuela's National Assembly measured inflation of about one point seven million percent in twenty eighteen. The government has cut zeros off the currency three times: three in two thousand and eight, five in twenty eighteen, and six in twenty twenty-one.

scenes.name: Venezuelan bolívar
scenes.headline: Oil wealth, spent and printed away
scenes.body: Expropriations, price controls and printed deficits, then the oil price crash.
scenes.voiceover: Venezuela has some of the world's biggest oil reserves. But nationalisations and price controls hurt production, the government funded huge deficits with printed money, and when the oil price crashed in twenty fourteen, the dollars stopped coming in. Sanctions made it worse.

scenes.headline: Rich in oil, poor in money
scenes.body: An oil giant whose currency collapsed anyway.
scenes.voiceover: It's a warning that natural resources alone can't protect a currency.

scenes.headline: Yugoslav dinar
scenes.voiceover: Number four. The Yugoslav dinar. Yugoslavia.

scenes.name: Yugoslav dinar
scenes.headline: A 500 billion dinar note

stat.label: Time for prices to double, January 1994

scenes.voiceover: In January nineteen ninety-four, prices in Yugoslavia doubled roughly every one and a half days. In one month they rose three hundred and thirteen million percent. The central bank printed a five hundred billion dinar note.

scenes.name: Yugoslav dinar
scenes.headline: Break-up, war and sanctions
scenes.body: The country split apart, the UN imposed sanctions, and the state printed money to pay for war and wages.
scenes.voiceover: As Yugoslavia broke apart, wars began in Croatia and Bosnia, the United Nations imposed sanctions, and much of the economy stopped working. The government printed money to pay soldiers and state salaries.

scenes.headline: Weimar papiermark
scenes.voiceover: Number three. The Weimar papiermark. Germany.

scenes.name: Weimar papiermark
scenes.headline: Prices doubled every 3.7 days

stat.label: Marks to one US dollar, November 1923

scenes.voiceover: By November nineteen twenty-three, one US dollar cost four point two trillion German marks. At the peak, prices doubled about every three point seven days. Workers were paid twice a day, and rushed to spend their wages before they lost value.

scenes.name: Weimar papiermark
scenes.headline: War debt, reparations and the Ruhr
scenes.body: WWI was paid for with debt; then came Versailles reparations and the 1923 Ruhr occupation.
scenes.voiceover: Germany paid for the First World War with debt, then owed huge reparations under the Treaty of Versailles. When France and Belgium occupied the Ruhr in nineteen twenty-three, the government printed money to pay striking workers. Confidence collapsed.

scenes.headline: The printing press ran day and night
scenes.body: Germany's mint couldn't print notes fast enough.
scenes.voiceover: The printing presses ran day and night, and still couldn't keep up.

scenes.headline: Zimbabwe dollar
scenes.voiceover: Number two. The Zimbabwe dollar. Zimbabwe.

scenes.name: Zimbabwe dollar
scenes.headline: A 100 trillion dollar note
scenes.voiceover: In November two thousand and eight, prices in Zimbabwe rose an estimated seventy-nine point six billion percent in a month, doubling about every twenty-five hours. In January two thousand and nine, the Reserve Bank issued a one hundred trillion dollar note.

scenes.name: Zimbabwe dollar
scenes.headline: Farms seized, money printed
scenes.body: Land seizures crushed farm output and tax revenue; deficits were paid with printed money.
scenes.voiceover: From two thousand, a fast-track land reform programme seized commercial farms, and food and export production collapsed. Spending on the war in the Congo and on patronage was funded by printing money, as tax revenue fell.

scenes.headline: Shelves empty. Shops closed.
scenes.body: In 2009 Zimbabwe dropped its own currency for the US dollar and the rand.
scenes.voiceover: In two thousand and nine, Zimbabwe gave up its own currency and started using the US dollar and the South African rand. Many Zimbabweans came to South Africa to survive.

scenes.headline: Hungarian pengő
scenes.voiceover: Number one. The Hungarian pengő. Hungary.

scenes.name: Hungarian pengő
scenes.headline: The worst hyperinflation ever recorded

stat.label: Time for prices to double, July 1946

scenes.voiceover: In July nineteen forty-six, prices in Hungary rose by forty-one thousand trillion percent in a single month. That's prices doubling every fifteen hours. It's the worst hyperinflation ever recorded.

scenes.name: Hungarian pengő
scenes.headline: War ruin, reparations, and printing
scenes.body: WWII destroyed industry; Hungary owed reparations and printed money to cope.
scenes.voiceover: The Second World War destroyed Hungary's factories, railways and bridges. The country owed war reparations, mainly to the Soviet Union, and the government printed money to keep going. The largest note ever printed was one hundred quintillion pengő. In August nineteen forty-six, the forint replaced it, and the forint is still Hungary's currency today.

scenes.headline: Greece 1944. Peru 1990. Brazil before 1994.
scenes.voiceover: Honourable mentions: Greece in nineteen forty-four, where prices rose thirteen thousand eight hundred percent in one month, Peru in nineteen ninety, and Brazil's string of failed currencies before the real in nineteen ninety-four.

scenes.headline: Governments printed money faster than the economy could grow.
scenes.voiceover: Every one of these failures has the same root. Governments printed money to pay for war, reparations or spending, faster than the economy could produce goods. Once people lost confidence, the collapse fed itself.

scenes.headline: Why central bank independence matters
scenes.body: The SA Reserve Bank's independence is protected by the Constitution.
scenes.voiceover: That's why South Africa's Constitution protects the independence of the Reserve Bank. Its job is to protect the value of the rand, not to fund the government.

scenes.headline: Which of these surprised you most?
scenes.voiceover: Which of these surprised you most? Tell us in the comments.
